note: The one table of private-value shapes. tools/release/pii-scan.py (the release gate over tracked files) and crates/zerocode-core/src/private_data.rs (the mask every kept worker hand-in passes through) both read this file, so what the gate refuses and what the keeper masks cannot drift apart. `find` is what a category looks like; `allow` fully matches a found value to forgive it; `skip` lists paths only the gate leaves unread; `why` is documentation. A regex here must stay inside the syntax Python's `re` and Rust's `regex` crate share (no look-around, no back-references).

rules.name: home-path
rules.says: a real account's home directory, written out or slugged into a session id
rules.why: Both separators, and a Rust string's doubled backslash. There is no `/home/` row: every `/home/` path in this tree is a container root (`codex-runtime-home/home/…`) or a role (`builder`, `codex`), so the row would be noise — a remote account's name is what the banished row and the diff catch.

rules.name: private-ip
rules.says: an address on a real private network (RFC 1918), which names an office
rules.why: The private subnets this repository's fixtures stand on: the two every manual uses for an example, and the single address that pins the RFC 1918 boundary itself. Loopback and link-local are not in `find` because they name the machine, never an office. The RFC 5737 documentation addresses (192.0.2/198.51.100/203.0.113) are not private, so `find` never reaches them.

rules.name: email
rules.says: a mailbox outside the reserved example domains — a real person or service
skip: third-party bundles and their authors' own copyright notices
rules.why: Reserved and fictional domains, the public code hosts a `git@` URL names, Google's own service-account example — and a retina asset (`icon@2x.png`, `128x128@2x.png`), whose `@2x` is a scale, not a mailbox.

rules.name: credential
rules.says: a token or key of a shape a provider actually issues, carrying a body
skip: third-party bundles carry minified strings of every shape
rules.why: A PEM header is a shape a test writes freely; only one carrying real base64 after it is a key: three wrapped runs, at any width a writer chose. `allow` is a fixture saying so in its own body; a leaked token never would.
